en: The Legend of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta Buddhavagga 7 I was a young brahmin, well-versed in the Vedas, and I was skilled in the three branches of knowledge. At that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Having heard of the fame of the Blessed One, I went to him. Having approached the Blessed One, I exchanged greetings with him. Having exchanged courteous and amiable greetings, I sat down to one side. As I was sitting there, I said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I am a young brahmin, well-versed in the Vedas, and skilled in the three branches of knowledge. Then the Blessed One spoke thus to me: “Young brahmin, what is the purpose of your being well-versed in the Vedas? What is the purpose of your skill in the three branches of knowledge? “I have heard, Master Gotama, that the Blessed One is omniscient and all-seeing, and that he knows all things without exception. I wish to hear from the Blessed One himself whether this is so or not. “Very well, young brahmin, listen and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, sir,” I replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One spoke thus: “Young brahmin, I am indeed omniscient and all-seeing, and I know all things without exception. However, it is not easy for me to answer your question directly. Rather, I shall ask you a question in return; answer as you see fit. “Ask, Master Gotama; I shall answer as I see fit. “Is it true, young brahmin, that you say: ‘I am a young brahmin, well-versed in the Vedas, and skilled in the three branches of knowledge’? “It is true, Master Gotama. “What do you think, young brahmin? Is the earth eternal, or is it not eternal? “I do not know this, Master Gotama. “What do you think, young brahmin? Is the world eternal, or is it not eternal? “I do not know this, Master Gotama. “What do you think, young brahmin? Does the Tathāgata exist after death, or does he not exist after death? “I do not know this, Master Gotama. “What do you think, young brahmin? Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death, or does he neither exist nor not exist after death? “I do not know this, Master Gotama. “Young brahmin, you say: ‘I am a young brahmin, well-versed in the Vedas, and skilled in the three branches of knowledge. Yet when asked about these matters, you say, ‘I do not know. How then can you claim to be well-versed in the Vedas and skilled in the three branches of knowledge? “Master Gotama, I have heard that the ancient seers, well-versed in the Vedas and skilled in the three branches of knowledge, did not know these things. Therefore, I too do not know them. “Very well, young brahmin. Just as those ancient seers were well-versed in the Vedas and skilled in the three branches of knowledge yet did not know these things, so too are you well-versed in the Vedas and skilled in the three branches of knowledge, yet you do not know these things. But, young brahmin, I know this: ‘This is suffering. I know this: ‘This is the origin of suffering. I know this: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. I know this: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Therefore, young brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall be one who knows suffering; I shall be one who knows the origin of suffering; I shall be one who knows the cessation of suffering; I shall be one who knows the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! It is as if someone were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.

Then the Blessed One, knowing my inclinations, my disposition, and my character, taught me the Dhamma in such a way that as I sat there, the spotless, immaculate eye of the Dhamma arose within me: “Whatever is subject to origination is subject to cessation. When the Dhamma-eye arose, I thought: “I have gained a great gain in that I have seen the Blessed One. Then I rose from my seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on my right, I departed. At that time, I was a householder named Puṇṇa, a wealthy man with vast riches and great wealth. I had a son named Mantāṇi. I gave that son, Mantāṇi, to the Blessed One as a novice. Having become a novice under the Blessed One, I dwelt practicing for my own benefit and for the benefit of others. Through diligent effort, I realized the goal of the holy life even in this very existence, having myself attained it through direct knowledge. I lived having realized: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. I became an arahant, one of the Great Elders. This is my elder-apadāna.
“A reciter, a bearer of mantras,
one who has gone to the further shore of the three Vedas—
I am preceded by my disciples.”
I approached that supreme among men.
Padumuttara, the Knower of the World,
the recipient of offerings;
The Great Sage briefly proclaimed my deed;
having heard that Dhamma, I—
Having paid homage to the Teacher and having raised my joined palms in reverence,
I departed facing the south.
Having heard it in brief,
I explained it in detail;
all the disciples were delighted.
Having heard me speak,
they dispelled their own views and gained confidence in the Buddha.
I teach both in brief and likewise in detail;
I am one who knows the method of the Abhidhamma.
Having made myself understood by all through the purification of the *kathāvatthu*,
I dwell free from taints.
In these five hundred eons,
there were four excellent illuminators,
endowed with the seven jewels.
The lords over the four continents;
the four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations;
"The six direct knowledges have been realized;
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed did the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta recite these verses.
The legend of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is the fifth.
